solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Shifting coffee table and PC provides surprising health benefits

definitions.note: singular phrase for plural benefits: the phenomenon as a whole

indicators.note: shifting the letters about means the words coffee table and PC are rearranged

explanation.surface: Rearranging the furniture and the computer apparently does wonders for your wellbeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shifting' rearranges COFFEE TABLE plus PC, thirteen letters in all.
explanation.definitionFit: The phenomenon in which a dummy treatment makes patients feel better, purely because they believe in it, gives unexpected health gains.

clue.text: One presenting a down-at-heel image?

parts.note: down-at-heel usually means shabby, but here the picture is literally down at heel level, chalked on the pedestrian walkway

explanation.surface: Someone who looks shabby and poor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down-at-heel' suggests a scruffy appearance; read literally, the image lies on the ground beneath passers-by's feet.
explanation.definitionFit: A street artist who draws chalk pictures on the footpath shows images at the level of people's feet.

clue.text: Poetic form master in eau de nil

indicators.note: in means the letters are found sitting inside the phrase eau de nil

explanation.surface: A poet skilled in verse forms dressed in a pale green shade.
explanation.walkthrough: Eau de nil is a pale greenish colour; the poet sits inside 'eau de nil'.
explanation.definitionFit: W. H. Auden, the Anglo-American poet, was famed for his technical mastery of verse forms from sonnet to villanelle.

clue.text: Advocate leaving set off

indicators.note: off in the sense of wrong or out of order means the letters of leaving set are rearranged

explanation.surface: A lawyer leaving after setting things in motion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' signals the anagram of LEAVING SET.
explanation.definitionFit: A zealous promoter of a cause, like a preacher of the gospel, is a champion or campaigner for it.

clue.text: Curate poetry written in Old English

indicators.note: written in means the poetry word is placed inside the abbreviation for Old English

parts.note: poetry is verse

explanation.surface: A clergyman's verse composed in the language of the Anglo-Saxons.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Curate' looks like the clergyman, but it is the verb used of exhibitions.
explanation.definitionFit: To curate an exhibition is to supervise and organise its selection, which is to supervise it.

clue.text: Documentary's bad fault when incorporating account

definitions.note: read as documentary is, with documentary the adjective (documentary evidence)

indicators.note: incorporating means taking in, so the rearranged fault takes the account letters inside it
bad here means messed up, so the letters of fault are rearranged

explanation.surface: A TV documentary has a serious flaw in its accounting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bad' rearranges into F-TUAL for 'when incorporating' to open. 'Documentary' is the adjective here, as in documentary evidence, with 's standing for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Documentary evidence is based on records and real events, so it is true and based on fact.

clue.text: Onset of extra time keeps football team going

indicators.note: keeps means holds, so the first letter of extra and the time letter hold the football team letters between them
the onset of a word is its beginning, so take the first letter of extra

parts.note: a football side has eleven players, XI in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: Extra time begins and the side keeps playing on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keeps' puts XI, a team of eleven, between E and T.
explanation.definitionFit: A going is a departure, the act of leaving, as in comings and goings.

clue.text: Drink down under while chap's getting stuck into meal

indicators.note: getting stuck into means wedged inside, so the pieces go inside the meal word

parts.note: tea is an evening or afternoon meal
as can mean while, as in 'as he spoke'
a chap is a man, with the 's kept

explanation.surface: An Australian has a drink while a bloke tucks into his dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting stuck into' is the container signal. 'Drink' is slang for the sea, and 'down under' means near Australia.
explanation.definitionFit: Colloquially the drink is the sea, and this one lies between Australia and New Zealand, the lands called down under.

clue.text: Mixing one surgeon's title up in midst of complex operation

indicators.note: in midst of means set right in the middle of the operation word

parts.note: integration is a mathematical operation, and can be done on complex functions

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the pieces read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: one is I in Roman numerals
British surgeons are addressed as Mr rather than Dr

explanation.surface: A surgeon's title gets muddled during a complicated procedure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' gives RMI, which 'in midst of' sets in the operation. 'Mixing' looks like part of the surface, but it is the definition. British surgeons are traditionally styled Mr, not Dr.
explanation.definitionFit: Peoples migrating among one another and intermingling is a mixing of populations.

clue.text: Spirit of old duke regularly seen in V&A

indicators.note: seen in means placed within, so the pieces go inside V and A

parts.note: the V&A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum, giving V and A

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter of duke

explanation.surface: The ghost of an old aristocrat haunts a London museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' takes D and K from DUKE; 'seen in' sets O and DK inside V and A. The V&A is London's Victoria and Albert Museum.
explanation.definitionFit: A spirit is a strong distilled drink, and this colourless Russian liquor is the classic example.

clue.text: Make ruddy new offenders put in long stretch of time

indicators.note: put in means placed inside, so new and offenders go inside the long time

parts.note: an eon is an immensely long period
crims is informal for criminals

explanation.surface: Fresh criminals are blushing as they are sent down for a long sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Put in' is the container signal. 'Stretch' suggests a prison term, but it is a span of time.
explanation.definitionFit: To turn something deep red, the colour of crimson, is to redden it or make it rosy.

clue.text: European party appropriating £1000?

indicators.note: appropriating means taking for itself, so the party word takes the money inside

parts.note: a masque is a masked ball or entertainment
a thousand pounds is one grand, written ONE G

explanation.surface: A European political party pockets a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Appropriating' puts ONE G inside MASQUE. G stands for a grand, slang for a thousand pounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A native of the principality of Monaco on the Riviera is a European by nationality.

clue.text: Leaves of the elder

definitions.meaning: the aromatic grey-green leaves of a kitchen herb used with onion in stuffing
a wise elder, a venerable person respected for wisdom

explanation.surface: Foliage from the elder tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The herb is used as leaves, and a wise old person or elder is a man of wisdom.

clue.text: Big AA Milne novel not too far-fetched

indicators.note: novel means new or unusual, so the letters of Big AA Milne are made into a new order

explanation.surface: A large A. A. Milne book that is quite believable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a book by Milne but signals rearranging BIG AA MILNE. A. A. Milne wrote Winnie-the-Pooh.
explanation.definitionFit: Something capable of being pictured in the mind is conceivable, so not too implausible.

clue.text: A small room amid New England housing

indicators.note: amid means in the middle of, so the pieces sit inside New England

parts.note: a cell is a small room, as in a prison or monastery

explanation.surface: A tiny room somewhere in a New England house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Housing' looks like homes, but it is the casing on an aircraft.
explanation.definitionFit: The streamlined casing that encloses an aircraft engine is a housing for it.

clue.text: Opener from county's team

parts.note: Cork is a county in Ireland, with the 's kept
a crew is a team, as of rowers

explanation.surface: A batsman who opens for a county side.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opener' suggests a cricket batsman, which the county team supports. Cork is an Irish county.
explanation.definitionFit: This spiral tool draws stoppers out of wine bottles, so it opens them.

clue.text: Chubby US mother avoiding starters and large chunk of bread

indicators.note: avoiding starters means each word loses its first letter

parts.note: plump means chubby
mum is mother

explanation.surface: A chubby American mother skipping the first courses and having a big piece of bread instead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Avoiding starters' removes the first letters of PLUMP, US and MUM. 'Bread' is slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread is slang for money, and a single big payment of money is a large chunk of it.

clue.text: Mark off pieces of furniture in stalls

definitions.note: stalls as a verb, stops or holds up

indicators.note: off means removed, so the letter for Mark comes away

parts.note: armrests are the parts of seats you lean your arms on
M is the abbreviation for Mark, also the old German currency

explanation.surface: Someone marking furniture in the theatre stalls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off' removes M from ARMRESTS. 'Stalls' looks like theatre seats, but it is the verb meaning halts.
explanation.definitionFit: To halt the progress of something, or check it, is to bring it to a stop.

clue.text: Seconds before profuse grovelling

parts.note: lavish means profuse or abundant

explanation.surface: A moment before effusive fawning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Before' places S ahead of LAVISH.
explanation.definitionFit: Grovelling behaviour is servile and submissive, like a slave's.

clue.text: Universal launch epic involving good outlaw

indicators.note: involving means taking in, so the epic word wraps round good and outlaw

parts.note: epic means big, on a grand scale
to outlaw something is to ban it

explanation.surface: An epic film whose hero is a good outlaw, released worldwide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Involving' opens the epic word after its I. 'Universal launch' is the start of the universe, not a worldwide film release.
explanation.definitionFit: Cosmologists hold that the universe began with a vast explosion, the moment the cosmos was set in motion.

clue.text: Tap on shoulder produces pain in the neck

parts.note: to tap a phone is to bug it
to shoulder a burden is to bear it

explanation.surface: A pat on the shoulder that causes a crick in the neck.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts BUG above BEAR; both are verbs, not a touch on the body.
explanation.definitionFit: A persistent source of annoyance or irritation is a pet hate.

clue.text: Voiced disapproval about uranium and source of banned material

indicators.note: about means around, so the disapproving sound goes round the uranium symbol

parts.note: tsk is the sound of disapproval
U is the chemical symbol for uranium

explanation.surface: Protesters objected to uranium and other prohibited substances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About' puts TSK round U. The banned material is ivory, not radioactive uranium.
explanation.definitionFit: The ivory trade is outlawed, and an elephant's long tooth is where ivory comes from.

clue.text: Notes alarming blunders before I answer

indicators.note: blunders means makes a mess of, so the letters of alarming are muddled

explanation.surface: Annotations that point out shocking mistakes before I respond.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blunders' looks like a noun, but it is the verb rearranging ALARMING, followed by I and A.
explanation.definitionFit: Scribbled comments in the margins of a book are notes.

clue.text: Tipped British director to take away Oscar

parts.note: David Lean directed Lawrence of Arabia

indicators.note: take away means remove, so the letter for Oscar leaves the word to

parts.note: O is Oscar in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: A British filmmaker was tipped to win an Academy Award.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take away Oscar' removes O from TO. 'Oscar' suggests the film award, but it is the radio code for O.
explanation.definitionFit: Something tipped is tilted or inclined to one side, past tense.

clue.text: Travel always upset painter

parts.note: to go is to travel

indicators.note: upset means turned over, so in a down clue always is read upwards

parts.note: ay is an old word for always

explanation.surface: Constant travel upsets an artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' reverses AY, an old word for ever, into YA.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco Goya was the Spanish court artist famous for The Third of May 1808.

clue.text: Half of day is boring dry lecture

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so the pieces bore into the dry word

parts.note: sere means dry or withered

indicators.note: half of takes the first half of the day name

parts.note: Monday is a day

explanation.surface: Half the day is wasted on a tedious lecture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half of' keeps the first three letters of the day, and 'boring' is the container signal. 'Boring' and 'dry' look like criticism of the lecture.
explanation.definitionFit: To lecture someone is to preach at them at tedious length.

clue.text: Snack made by British Muslim pilgrim

parts.note: a haji is a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca

explanation.surface: A snack cooked by a British Muslim who has been to Mecca.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Made by' just links B and HAJI.
explanation.definitionFit: A spicy Indian fritter of vegetables in gram-flour batter is eaten as a starter or nibble.

clue.text: Heard if cooking celebrity is worn down by exposure

indicators.note: heard means the words are said aloud, giving a sound-alike

parts.note: if is whether, and the cooking celebrity is Mrs Beeton, the Victorian cookery writer

explanation.surface: A TV chef has been worn out by too much publicity.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heard' sounds out WHETHER (if) plus BEETON. Mrs Beeton wrote a famous Victorian book of household management and cookery.
explanation.definitionFit: A face or building battered by wind, rain and sun is weathered and roughened by the elements.
